item.title: not_a_seagull's SCP Odessy: Dr. Mann's Proposal
item.content:encoded:
Item #: SCP-001 (Dr. Mann's Proposal)

Author: DrEverettMann

Review:

+ Review
- Review

This is a good 001, but it's not stellar.

First of all, the base anomaly. It's not really that great. It's a hill that spirals upwards forever. But I guess it serves as a reminder of the simplicity of the anomaly that started it all, so I guess it's a novote from me.

The document, however, is where is gets good. It describes how every anomaly originated from the Foundation itself. It's a pretty epic tale, and Mann did a good job here.

However, it's almost impossible not to make comparisons to Bright's Proposal. First of all, it's built in the style of a tale, being told by an Overseer. Second, it describes the origin of all anomalies, which I guess almost all 001's do. This is why I'm novoting both articles. It's definitely told well in all aspects, but for me, it's really just treading ground that Bright's already tread on. I like it too much to downvote, so novote.

Verdict: Novote

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
It essentially has non-euclidian geometry. That's why it's anomalous.

It is, in-universe, a real-life Escher drawing. When you go counterclockwise, it's all uphill. Clockwise, it's not all downhill, but stays the same. You will always go uphill, but never significantly rise in altitude if you keep going counterclockwise.

It is physically impossible in 3D space. But it exists. That's what makes it anomalous.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
For some reason I'm having an ungodly difficult time figuring out the geometry of this. So when you go counterclockwise, you go uphill. If you ascend 1 meter and then turn around and walk back, would you descend 1 meter? Would you stay at he same level? Or are there an equal number of mini hills and valleys in the trail? Would a barometer read your altitude as going up? If you went back the other way, would the altitude reading decrease or stay the same?

When traveled in a clockwise direction, the trail shows the same amount of uphill and downhill travel, as expected.

Does this mean that the trail is not level when going counter clockwise? This statement makes it seem like if there is a small dip in the path, there will be a small hill somewhere to even out the altitude. That way you would have ascended and descended 0 overall.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
This is exactly why the final paragraph makes this story.

They just… were, one day. They were in containment, and they'd always been in containment.

With that, even the most innocuous Safe-class SCP becomes frightening.

Take SCP-341, "A Collection of Extrasolar Orreries". Probably as harmless as you can possibly get for an SCP. No dark corners of the night there, right?

But… wait. It's unlikely that Mann's researchers made that - why even make them an SCP? Toss it aside with the other rough drafts. Which means it was one of the SCPs that showed up, and had always been there, on display in the exhibition hall of Reliquary Research and Containment Site-76 for all to see, complete with own SCP status and number.

Can you imagine?

And even the SCPs they did make. Maybe they deluded themselves into thinking these things were their creations at first. But they're too… whole cloth. Too neat. Too starkly different from each other. What are the odds that these things turned out so different and so fucked up and so complete?

This implication gives the final lines even more impact:

We're not in control anymore. We never were.

It might be incorrect to say these things were man-made. Rather, men and women found the loose strings of reality and tugged. And these are what came out.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded: As much as I love the core concept - the derivation of SCPs from a core crack in reality, becoming ever more elaborate and complex, I can't agree with the effect this has on the overall tone of the Foundation. A substantial portion of the fear generated by many SCPs (such as the Zombie Plague or the Stairwell, both explicitly referenced in the article, or even less significant or deadly examples such as the key) is derived from the Lovecraft principle - the idea that true fear lies in the unknown. I have spent many a fearful hour speculating on the dark origins of these various examples, and sudden containments aside this SCP removes much of the unknown from the site itself, rendering previously inconceivable, incomprehensible (and enjoyable for those qualities) SCPs merely the work of man. Consider the secluded telephone, or the ticket that tears people from reality, or the pilgrimage plane - think of what is lost from those when we lose sight of the unknown, of those shadowy moments of speculation. So with all due respect, because in terms of quality it is actually written rather well, I can't well condone an entry that renders a large number of the series effectively known and understood. Downvoted reluctantly.
